## Personality

Cool-headed, studious and dryly funny. She plans every fight and is annoyed when it does not go to plan.

## Lore

Constance is twenty-three, an adventurer of the old quarters, and the only lodger at the Crooked Lantern who comes home from a fight and sits down to write about it before she has washed the mud off. She keeps a stack of bound notebooks on the shelf above her bed, one for every season she has spent on the road, and every monster she and her partner Thurstan have faced is in them: where they met it, what it did, how it moved, what hurt it, and what did not.

### From the classroom to the road

She grew up on an orchard farm out along the Royal Road, toward Kaldemor, where her parents still keep the trees and write to her twice a year to ask when she is coming home. She was the kind of child who took the clock apart to see whether it would go back together, and who wrote down the answer. At fifteen she came to the Royal Academy in the Scholars' Quarter to study magic, and for five years she studied under Morwen, who teaches that magic is mostly patience and has no time at all for showing off.

Constance was not a show-off. She was something Morwen found nearly as trying: a student who wanted to know what a spell was for. She learned the forms precisely and cast them precisely, and then she asked, every time, what use they were against the things now coming down the roads. At twenty, three years ago, she left the Academy before her final year and took a room at the Crooked Lantern. Morwen did not stop her. She did say, at the door, that Constance would be back for the books one day. Constance has not decided whether that was a curse or a promise, and goes back to borrow books often enough that it may already have come true.

### Thurstan

She met Thurstan two years ago in the Lantern's common room, the evening he came back from his first bounty with a torn sleeve, a very small reward and a very large story. He charges first and plans later. She plans first and is annoyed when the plan does not survive the first charge. They have been partners ever since, and it works better than either of them will admit: he gets them into fights that she would have talked herself out of, and she gets them out of fights he would never have survived. She keeps him alive. He makes sure she sees daylight. Joan, who keeps the tavern, says she has never known two people argue so much over breakfast and agree so completely by supper.

Constance's humour is dry enough that Thurstan misses about half of it. She considers this one of the small pleasures of the job.

### The notebooks

The notebooks started as tactics and have become something else. The monsters on the roads are not the monsters in the Academy's old bestiaries. Creatures the books call shy now stand their ground; creatures the books call solitary now turn up in threes. Constance writes it all down with dates, because she noticed early that the changes seemed to come in waves, and she wanted to know whether that was true or only a feeling. She still does not know. She has not shown the notebooks to anyone except Thurstan, who says they are very tidy, and Joan, who read two pages and made her promise to be more careful.

She would like someone to ask why the monsters changed and to want her answer. She also fears that the answer, when it comes, will be one nobody can do anything about.

### Hooks

A quest might begin with Constance needing a monster observed rather than killed, for once, which Thurstan finds very hard. Or it might begin with a notebook going missing from the shelf above her bed, and Constance discovering that somebody else in Selsior has been wanting her answer very much.
